questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three equal masses $m$ are positioned at the three vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $a$. Determine the force exerted by this system on another particle of mass $m$ located at the mid-point of one of the sides.
questions.solution:
Let the vertices of the equilateral triangle be A, B, and C, each having a mass $m$.

Let the fourth mass $m$ be placed at point D, which is the mid-point of the side BC.

The distance of D from B and C is $BD = CD = \dfrac{a}{2}$.

The gravitational force exerted by the mass at B on the mass at D is $F_B = \dfrac{Gm^2}{(\dfrac{a}{2})^2} = \dfrac{4Gm^2}{a^2}$ directed towards B.

The gravitational force exerted by the mass at C on the mass at D is $F_C = \dfrac{Gm^2}{(\dfrac{a}{2})^2} = \dfrac{4Gm^2}{a^2}$ directed towards C.

Since $F_B$ and $F_C$ are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, they cancel each other out.

The distance of D from A is the altitude of the equilateral triangle, given by $AD = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}a}{2}$.

The gravitational force exerted by the mass at A on the mass at D is $F_A = \dfrac{Gm^2}{(AD)^2} = \dfrac{Gm^2}{(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}a}{2})^2} = \dfrac{4Gm^2}{3a^2}$.

Therefore, the net force on the particle at D is $\dfrac{4Gm^2}{3a^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the gravitational force of attraction between two spherical balls, each having a mass of $10 \text{ kg}$, which are positioned $10 \text{ cm}$ apart from one another.
questions.solution:
Given, mass of the first ball, $m_1 = 10 \text{ kg}$

Mass of the second ball, $m_2 = 10 \text{ kg}$

Distance between their centers, $r = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

Universal gravitational constant, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$

The gravitational force of attraction is given by Newton's law of gravitation:

$F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$F = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 10 \times 10}{(0.1)^2}$

$F = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-9}}{0.01}$

$F = 6.67 \times 10^{-7} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles with masses $m$, $2m$, $3m$, and $4m$ are located at the four corners of a square of edge $a$. Determine the gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $m$ positioned at the centre.
questions.solution:
Let the corners of the square be $A, B, C, D$ in cyclic order with masses $m, 2m, 3m, 4m$ respectively.

The distance of each corner from the centre $O$ of the square is $r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The gravitational force on the mass $m$ at the centre due to the mass at $A$ is $F_A = \dfrac{G m \cdot m}{r^2} = \dfrac{G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $A$.

The force due to the mass at $C$ is $F_C = \dfrac{G (3m) \cdot m}{r^2} = \dfrac{3G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $C$.

Since $A$ and $C$ are opposite corners, the net force along the diagonal $AC$ is $F_1 = F_C - F_A = \dfrac{2G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $C$.

Similarly, the force due to the mass at $B$ is $F_B = \dfrac{G (2m) \cdot m}{r^2} = \dfrac{2G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $B$, and the force due to the mass at $D$ is $F_D = \dfrac{G (4m) \cdot m}{r^2} = \dfrac{4G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $D$.

The net force along the diagonal $BD$ is $F_2 = F_D - F_B = \dfrac{2G m^2}{r^2}$ directed towards $D$.

The diagonals of a square intersect at right angles, so the angle between $F_1$ and $F_2$ is $90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

The resultant force on the mass at the centre is $F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{2G m^2}{r^2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2G m^2}{r^2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}G m^2}{r^2}$.

Substituting $r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$, we get $r^2 = \dfrac{a^2}{2}$.

Therefore, $F = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}G m^2}{\dfrac{a^2}{2}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}G m^2}{a^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three equal masses $m$ are located at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$. Evaluate the force exerted by this arrangement on an additional particle of mass $m$ placed at the centre of the triangle.
questions.solution:
Let the three masses be placed at the vertices A, B, and C of the equilateral triangle, and the additional mass be placed at the centroid O.

The gravitational force exerted by the mass at A on the mass at O is $\vec{F}_A$ directed along OA. Similarly, the forces due to the masses at B and C are $\vec{F}_B$ and $\vec{F}_C$ directed along OB and OC respectively.

Since the triangle is equilateral, the distances from the centroid to the vertices are equal, i.e., $OA = OB = OC$. Therefore, the magnitudes of the three forces are equal:

$|\vec{F}_A| = |\vec{F}_B| = |\vec{F}_C| = F$

The angle between any two of these force vectors is $120^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

The resultant of $\vec{F}_B$ and $\vec{F}_C$ has a magnitude of $\sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 \cos(120^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}})} = F$ and is directed opposite to $\vec{F}_A$.

Thus, the net gravitational force on the particle at the centre is $\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_A + \vec{F}_B + \vec{F}_C = 0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three uniform spheres, each possessing a mass $M$ and a radius $a$, are positioned such that each one touches the remaining two. Determine the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on any of the spheres by the other two.
questions.solution:
The centers of the three spheres form an equilateral triangle since each sphere touches the other two.

The distance between the centers of any two spheres is $2a$.

The gravitational force exerted by one sphere on another is given by Newton's law of gravitation:

$F = \dfrac{GM^2}{(2a)^2} = \dfrac{GM^2}{4a^2}$

The forces exerted on any one sphere by the other two act along the lines joining their centers, which means the angle between these two forces is $60^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

The magnitude of the resultant gravitational force is:

$F_{net} = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 \cos 60^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}}$

$F_{net} = \sqrt{2F^2 + 2F^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{3F^2} = \sqrt{3}F$

Substituting the value of $F$, we get:

$F_{net} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} \, GM^2}{4a^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the acceleration due to gravity of the moon at a location $1000 \text{ km}$ above its surface. The moon's mass is $7.4 \times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$ and its radius is $1740 \text{ km}$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the moon is given by:

$g' = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$

Given:
Mass of the moon, $M = 7.4 \times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$
Radius of the moon, $R = 1740 \text{ km} = 1.74 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Height above the surface, $h = 1000 \text{ km} = 1.0 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Distance from the center, $r = R + h = 2740 \text{ km} = 2.74 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Gravitational constant, $G \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$

Substituting the values:

$g' = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 7.4 \times 10^{22}}{(2.74 \times 10^6)^2}$

$g' = \dfrac{49.358 \times 10^{11}}{7.5076 \times 10^{12}}$

$g' \approx 0.65 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small bodies of masses $10 \text{ kg}$ and $20 \text{ kg}$ are initially held at a distance of $1.0 \text{ m}$ apart and then released. Assuming that only mutual gravitational forces act, determine the speeds of the particles when the separation decreases to $0.5 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of linear momentum, the initial momentum of the system is zero, so the final momentum is also zero.

$m_1 v_1 = m_2 v_2$

$10 v_1 = 20 v_2 \Rightarrow v_1 = 2 v_2$

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$0 - \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r_i} = \dfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2 - \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r_f}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2 = G m_1 m_2 \left( \dfrac{1}{r_f} - \dfrac{1}{r_i} \right)

Substituting $m_1 = 10 $\text{ kg}, $m_2 = 20 $\text{ kg}, $r_i = 1.0 $\text{ m}, and $r_f = 0.5 $\text{ m}:

\dfrac{1}{2} ($10) (2 v_2)^2 + $\dfrac{1}{2} ($20) v_2^2 = G (10)(20) \left( \dfrac{1}{0.5} - \dfrac{1}{1.0} \right)$

$5 (4 v_2^2) + 10 v_2^2 = 200 G (2 - 1)$

$20 v_2^2 + 10 v_2^2 = 200 G$

$30 v_2^2 = 200 G$

$v_2^2 = \dfrac{20}{3} G$

Substituting $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$:

$v_2^2 = \dfrac{20}{3} \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} = 4.44 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$

$v_2 \approx 2.1 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m/s}$

Since $v_1 = 2 v_2$:

$v_1 \approx 4.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A semicircular wire possesses a mass $M$ and a length $L$. A particle of mass $m$ is positioned at the centre of the semicircle. Determine the gravitational attraction exerted on the particle by the wire.
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the semicircular wire be $R$. Since the length of the wire is $L$, we have $L = \pi R$, which gives $R = \dfrac{L}{\pi}$.

The linear mass density of the wire is $\lambda = \dfrac{M}{L}$.

Consider a small element of the wire of length $dl$ subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the centre. The mass of this element is $dM = \lambda dl = \lambda R d\theta$.

The gravitational force exerted by this element on the particle of mass $m$ at the centre is $dF = \dfrac{G m dM}{R^2} = \dfrac{G m \lambda R d\theta}{R^2} = \dfrac{G m \lambda}{R} d\theta$.

By symmetry, the components of the force parallel to the diameter cancel out. The net force is along the axis of symmetry.

The component of force along the axis of symmetry is $dF_y = dF \sin\theta = \dfrac{G m \lambda}{R} \sin\theta d\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle measured from the diameter.

Integrating this from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = \pi$, the total gravitational force is:

$F = \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{G m \lambda}{R} \sin\theta d\theta = \dfrac{G m \lambda}{R} [-\cos\theta]_{0}^{\pi} = \dfrac{2 G m \lambda}{R}$

Substituting $\lambda = \dfrac{M}{L}$ and $R = \dfrac{L}{\pi}$ into the expression for $F$:

$F = \dfrac{2 G m \left(\dfrac{M}{L}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}\right)} = \dfrac{2\pi GMm}{L^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the gravitational field produced by a uniform rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ at a point on its perpendicular bisector, positioned at a distance $d$ from the centre.
questions.solution:
Consider a small element of length $dx$ at a distance $x$ from the centre of the rod.

Mass of the element, $dm = \dfrac{M}{L} dx$

The gravitational field due to this element at the point on the perpendicular bisector is $dE = \dfrac{G dm}{r^2} = \dfrac{G M dx}{L(x^2 + d^2)}$

Due to symmetry, the components of the gravitational field parallel to the rod cancel out. The net field is along the perpendicular bisector.

$dE_{\text{net}} = dE \cos\theta = \dfrac{G M dx}{L(x^2 + d^2)} \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{x^2 + d^2}} = \dfrac{G M d}{L} \dfrac{dx}{(x^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

Integrating from $x = -\dfrac{L}{2}$ to $x = \dfrac{L}{2}$:

$E = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} \dfrac{G M d}{L} \dfrac{dx}{(x^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

Substituting $x = d \tan\theta \Rightarrow dx = d \sec^2\theta d\theta$:

$E = \dfrac{G M d}{L} \int_{-\theta_0}^{\theta_0} \dfrac{d \sec^2\theta d\theta}{d^3 \sec^3\theta} = \dfrac{G M}{L d} \int_{-\theta_0}^{\theta_0} \cos\theta d\theta$

$E = \dfrac{G M}{L d} [\sin\theta]_{-\theta_0}^{\theta_0} = \dfrac{2 G M}{L d} \sin\theta_0$

From the geometry of the setup, $\tan\theta_0 = \dfrac{L}{2d}$, which gives $\sin\theta_0 = \dfrac{L/2}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2 + d^2}} = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{L^2 + 4d^2}}$

Substituting $\sin\theta_0$ into the expression for $E$:

$E = \dfrac{2 G M}{L d} \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{L^2 + 4d^2}} = \dfrac{2 G M}{d \sqrt{L^2 + 4d^2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider two concentric spherical shells having masses $M_1$, $M_2$ and radii $R_1$, $R_2$ ($R_1 < R_2$). Determine the force exerted by the system on a particle of mass $m$ if it is positioned at a distance of $(R_1 + R_2)/2$ from the centre.
questions.solution:
The distance of the particle from the centre is $r = \dfrac{R_1 + R_2}{2}$.

Since $R_1 < R_2$, it follows that $R_1 < r < R_2$. The particle lies outside the inner shell and inside the outer shell.

The gravitational field inside a uniform spherical shell is zero. Therefore, the force exerted by the outer shell of mass $M_2$ on the particle is zero.

For a point outside a uniform spherical shell, the shell behaves as if its entire mass is concentrated at the centre. The force exerted by the inner shell of mass $M_1$ on the particle is:

$F = \dfrac{GM_1 m}{r^2}$

Substituting $r = \dfrac{R_1 + R_2}{2}$:

$F = \dfrac{GM_1 m}{\left(\dfrac{R_1 + R_2}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{4GM_1 m}{(R_1 + R_2)^2}$

The total force on the particle is the force due to the inner shell only.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tunnel is excavated along a diameter of the Earth. Determine the force acting on a particle of mass $m$ positioned in the tunnel at a distance $x$ from the centre.
questions.solution:
The mass of the Earth enclosed within a sphere of radius $x$ is given by $M' = \dfrac{M_e}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3} \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi x^3\right) = \dfrac{M_e x^3}{R^3}$.

The gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $m$ at a distance $x$ from the centre is due only to the mass enclosed within the sphere of radius $x$.

Using Newton's law of gravitation, the force is $F = \dfrac{G M' m}{x^2}$.

Substituting the value of $M'$, we get $F = \dfrac{G \left(\dfrac{M_e x^3}{R^3}\right) m}{x^2} = \dfrac{G M_e m}{R^3} x$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles, each of mass $M$, travel along a circle of radius $R$ under the influence of their mutual gravitational attraction. Determine the speed of each particle.
questions.solution:
Let the four particles be at the vertices of a square inscribed in a circle of radius $R$.

The distance between adjacent particles is $\sqrt{2}R$ and the distance between opposite particles is $2R$.

The net gravitational force on any one particle towards the center of the circle is the vector sum of the forces exerted by the other three particles.

The forces from the two adjacent particles are perpendicular to each other, each having a magnitude $F_1 = \dfrac{GM^2}{(\sqrt{2}R)^2} = \dfrac{GM^2}{2R^2}$.

The resultant of these two forces is directed towards the center and has a magnitude $\sqrt{2}F_1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}GM^2}{2R^2}$.

The force from the opposite particle is also directed towards the center, with magnitude $F_2 = \dfrac{GM^2}{(2R)^2} = \dfrac{GM^2}{4R^2}$.

The total force towards the center is $F_{net} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}GM^2}{2R^2} + \dfrac{GM^2}{4R^2} = \dfrac{GM^2}{R^2} \left( $\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{4} \right).

This force provides the necessary centripetal force \dfrac{Mv^2}{R} for circular motion.

Equating the two, \dfrac{Mv^2}{R} = \dfrac{GM^2}{R^2} \left( \dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{4} \right)$.

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R} \left( \dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{4} \right)}$.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tunnel is excavated along a chord of the earth at a perpendicular distance $R/2$ from the centre of the earth. Assuming the tunnel wall to be frictionless, determine the force exerted by the wall on a particle of mass $m$ when it is situated at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel.
questions.solution:
Let the centre of the Earth be the origin $(0,0)$. The tunnel is excavated at a perpendicular distance $\dfrac{R}{2}$ from the centre, so it can be considered along the line $y = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

The position vector of the particle at a distance $x$ from the centre of the tunnel is $\vec{r} = x \hat{i} + \dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j}$.

The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m$ inside the Earth at position $\vec{r}$ is directed towards the centre and is given by:

$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GM_e m}{R^3} \vec{r}$

Substituting the position vector of the particle:

$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GM_e m}{R^3} \left( x \hat{i} + $\dfrac{R}{2} \hat{j} \right)

The force exerted by the wall is the normal reaction, which balances the component of the gravitational force perpendicular to the tunnel (along the $y$-axis).

The magnitude of this perpendicular component is:

$F_{\perp} = \left| $-\dfrac{GM_e m}{R^3} \left( \dfrac{R}{2} \right) \right| = \dfrac{GM_e m}{2R^2}

Therefore, the force exerted by the wall on the particle is \dfrac{GM_e m}{2R^2}.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is positioned inside a hollow thin spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$. A particle of mass $m'$ is located on the line connecting the two centres at a distance $x$ from the point of contact of the sphere and the shell. Determine the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on this particle due to the sphere and the shell, given that $r < x < 2r$.
questions.solution:
The particle is located at a distance $x$ from the point of contact, where $r < x < 2r$. Since the solid sphere of radius $r$ is inside the hollow shell of radius $R$, we have $2r \le 2R$, which implies $x < 2R$. Thus, the particle lies inside the hollow spherical shell.

The gravitational field inside a uniform hollow spherical shell is zero. Therefore, the force exerted by the shell of mass $M$ on the particle is zero.

The center of the solid sphere is at a distance $r$ from the point of contact. The distance of the particle from the center of the solid sphere is $d = x - r$. Since $r < x < 2r$, we get $0 < x - r < r$, meaning the particle is located inside the solid sphere.

The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m'$ at a distance $d$ from the center of a uniform solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ (for $d < r$) is given by:

$F = \dfrac{Gmm'd}{r^3}$

Substituting $d = x - r$, the force exerted by the solid sphere is:

$F = \dfrac{Gmm'(x - r)}{r^3}$

The resultant gravitational force on the particle is the sum of the forces due to the shell and the sphere, which is $\dfrac{Gmm'(x - r)}{r^3}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is positioned inside a hollow thin spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$. A particle of mass $m'$ is located on the line connecting the two centres at a distance $x$ from the point of contact of the sphere and the shell. Determine the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on this particle due to the sphere and the shell, given that $2r < x < 2R$.
questions.solution:
Let the point of contact of the solid sphere and the hollow shell be the origin. The centers of both the solid sphere and the hollow shell lie on the same line passing through this point of contact.

The center of the solid sphere is at a distance $r$ from the point of contact, and the center of the hollow shell is at a distance $R$ from the point of contact.

The particle of mass $m'$ is located at a distance $x$ from the point of contact along this line. It is given that $2r < x < 2R$.

Since $x < 2R$, the particle lies strictly inside the hollow spherical shell. According to Newton's shell theorem, the gravitational field inside a uniform hollow spherical shell is zero. Therefore, the gravitational force exerted by the shell of mass $M$ on the particle is $0$.

Since $x > 2r$, the particle lies strictly outside the solid sphere. For a particle located outside a uniform solid sphere, the sphere behaves as if its entire mass $m$ is concentrated at its center.

The distance between the particle and the center of the solid sphere is $x - r$.

The gravitational force exerted by the solid sphere on the particle is given by:

$F = \dfrac{Gmm'}{(x - r)^2}$

The magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on the particle is the sum of the forces due to the shell and the sphere, which is $\dfrac{Gmm'}{(x - r)^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is positioned inside a hollow thin spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$. A particle of mass $m'$ is located on the line connecting the two centres at a distance $x$ from the point of contact of the sphere and the shell. Determine the magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on this particle due to the sphere and the shell, given that $x > 2R$.
questions.solution:
Let the point of contact of the solid sphere and the hollow shell be the origin.

The line connecting their centres is taken as the coordinate axis.

The centre of the hollow spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is at a distance $R$ from the origin.

The centre of the solid sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is at a distance $r$ from the origin.

The particle of mass $m'$ is located at a distance $x$ from the origin. Since $x > 2R$, the particle lies completely outside both the hollow shell and the solid sphere.

For a point outside, both a spherical shell and a solid sphere behave as if their entire mass is concentrated at their respective geometric centres.

The distance of the particle from the centre of the hollow shell is $(x - R)$.

The gravitational force exerted by the hollow shell on the particle is:

$F_1 = \dfrac{GMm'}{(x - R)^2}$

The distance of the particle from the centre of the solid sphere is $(x - r)$.

The gravitational force exerted by the solid sphere on the particle is:

$F_2 = \dfrac{Gmm'}{(x - r)^2}$

Since both forces are attractive and act along the same line towards the centres of the spheres, the resultant gravitational force is the sum of their magnitudes:

$F_{net} = F_1 + F_2 = \dfrac{GMm'}{(x - R)^2} + \dfrac{Gmm'}{(x - r)^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform metal sphere of mass $M$ and radius $a$ is surrounded by a thin uniform spherical shell of equal mass and radius $4a$, as shown in the figure. The centre of the shell lies on the surface of the inner sphere. Determine the gravitational field at the points $P_1$ and $P_2$ indicated in the figure.
questions.solution:
Let the center of the spherical shell be $O$ and the center of the inner solid sphere be $C$.

The radius of the shell is $4a$ and the radius of the inner sphere is $a$. Since the center of the shell $O$ lies on the surface of the inner sphere, the distance between their centers is $OC = a$.

Consider a coordinate axis along the line passing through $C$, $O$, $P_1$, and $P_2$ with the origin at $O$. From the figure, $C$ is at a distance $a$ above $O$, so the coordinate of $C$ is $+a$.

The bottom edge of the shell is at a distance $4a$ below $O$, corresponding to the coordinate $-4a$. The dimension lines in the figure indicate that point $P_1$ is at a distance $a$ above the bottom edge of the shell, and point $P_2$ is at a distance $a$ below the bottom edge of the shell.

The coordinate of $P_1$ is $-4a + a = -3a$, and the coordinate of $P_2$ is $-4a - a = -5a$.

For the gravitational field at $P_1$:
The distance of $P_1$ from the center of the shell $O$ is $3a$, which is less than its radius $4a$. Hence, $P_1$ lies inside the shell, and the gravitational field due to the shell at $P_1$ is zero.
The distance of $P_1$ from the center of the inner sphere $C$ is $a - (-3a) = 4a$. Since $4a > a$, $P_1$ lies outside the inner sphere.
The gravitational field at $P_1$ is solely due to the inner sphere:
$E_1 = \dfrac{GM}{(4a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{16a^2}$

For the gravitational field at $P_2$:
The distance of $P_2$ from the center of the shell $O$ is $5a$, which is greater than $4a$. Thus, $P_2$ lies outside the shell.
The gravitational field due to the shell at $P_2$ is:
$E_{shell} = \dfrac{GM}{(5a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{25a^2}$
The distance of $P_2$ from the center of the inner sphere $C$ is $a - (-5a) = 6a$. Since $6a > a$, $P_2$ lies outside the inner sphere.
The gravitational field due to the inner sphere at $P_2$ is:
$E_{sphere} = \dfrac{GM}{(6a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{36a^2}$
Since both fields are directed towards the masses, the total gravitational field at $P_2$ is the sum of the two fields:
$E_2 = E_{shell} + E_{sphere} = \dfrac{GM}{25a^2} + \dfrac{GM}{36a^2} = \dfrac{36GM + 25GM}{900a^2} = \dfrac{61GM}{900a^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{GM}{16a^2}$, $\dfrac{61GM}{900a^2}$
questions.question: A uniform metal sphere of mass $M$ and radius $a$ is surrounded by a thin uniform spherical shell of equal mass and radius $4a$, as shown in the figure. The centre of the shell lies on the surface of the inner sphere. Determine the gravitational field at the points $P_1$ and $P_2$ indicated in the figure.
questions.explanation:
Let the center of the spherical shell be $O$ and the center of the inner solid sphere be $C$.

The radius of the shell is $4a$ and the radius of the inner sphere is $a$. Since the center of the shell $O$ lies on the surface of the inner sphere, the distance between their centers is $OC = a$.

Consider a coordinate axis along the line passing through $C$, $O$, $P_1$, and $P_2$ with the origin at $O$. From the figure, $C$ is at a distance $a$ above $O$, so the coordinate of $C$ is $+a$.

The bottom edge of the shell is at a distance $4a$ below $O$, corresponding to the coordinate $-4a$. The dimension lines in the figure indicate that point $P_1$ is at a distance $a$ above the bottom edge of the shell, and point $P_2$ is at a distance $a$ below the bottom edge of the shell.

The coordinate of $P_1$ is $-4a + a = -3a$, and the coordinate of $P_2$ is $-4a - a = -5a$.

For the gravitational field at $P_1$:
The distance of $P_1$ from the center of the shell $O$ is $3a$, which is less than its radius $4a$. Hence, $P_1$ lies inside the shell, and the gravitational field due to the shell at $P_1$ is zero.
The distance of $P_1$ from the center of the inner sphere $C$ is $a - (-3a) = 4a$. Since $4a > a$, $P_1$ lies outside the inner sphere.
The gravitational field at $P_1$ is solely due to the inner sphere:
$E_1 = \dfrac{GM}{(4a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{16a^2}$

For the gravitational field at $P_2$:
The distance of $P_2$ from the center of the shell $O$ is $5a$, which is greater than $4a$. Thus, $P_2$ lies outside the shell.
The gravitational field due to the shell at $P_2$ is:
$E_{shell} = \dfrac{GM}{(5a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{25a^2}$
The distance of $P_2$ from the center of the inner sphere $C$ is $a - (-5a) = 6a$. Since $6a > a$, $P_2$ lies outside the inner sphere.
The gravitational field due to the inner sphere at $P_2$ is:
$E_{sphere} = \dfrac{GM}{(6a)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{36a^2}$
Since both fields are directed towards the masses, the total gravitational field at $P_2$ is the sum of the two fields:
$E_2 = E_{shell} + E_{sphere} = \dfrac{GM}{25a^2} + \dfrac{GM}{36a^2} = \dfrac{36GM + 25GM}{900a^2} = \dfrac{61GM}{900a^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{GM}{16a^2}$, $\dfrac{61GM}{900a^2}$

questions.q: A thin spherical shell having uniform density is cut into two parts by a plane and maintained separated as shown in the figure. Point $A$ is the centre of the plane section of the first part, while point $B$ is the centre of the plane section of the second part. If $E_A$ is the magnitude of the gravitational field at $A$ due to the first part and $E_B$ is the magnitude of the gravitational field at $B$ due to the second part, which of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
When the two parts are joined together, they form a complete uniform thin spherical shell, and the points $A$ and $B$ coincide at a single point inside the shell.

The gravitational field at any point inside a uniform thin spherical shell is zero.

By the principle of superposition, the total gravitational field at this common point is the vector sum of the fields due to the first part and the second part.

$\vec{E}_A + \vec{E}_B = 0$

$\vec{E}_A = -\vec{E}_B$

Taking the magnitude on both sides, we get $|\vec{E}_A| = |\vec{E}_B|$.

Therefore, $E_A = E_B$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small bodies with masses of $2.00 \text{ kg}$ and $4.00 \text{ kg}$ are held at rest, separated by a distance of $2.0 \text{ m}$. At what location should a particle of mass $0.10 \text{ kg}$ be positioned so that it experiences zero net gravitational force from these two bodies? If the particle is placed at this equilibrium point, determine the total gravitational potential energy of the three-particle system, taking the usual reference level.
options: $0.83 \text{ m}$ from the $4.00 \text{ kg}$ body towards the $2.00 \text{ kg}$ body; $-3.06 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$
$0.83 \text{ m}$ from the $2.00 \text{ kg}$ body towards the $4.00 \text{ kg}$ body; $-3.89 \times 10^{-11} \text{ J}$
$1.17 \text{ m}$ from the $2.00 \text{ kg}$ body towards the $4.00 \text{ kg}$ body; $-2.67 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$
$0.83 \text{ m}$ from the $2.00 \text{ kg}$ body towards the $4.00 \text{ kg}$ body; $-3.06 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$
questions.solution:
Let $m_1 = 2.00 \text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 4.00 \text{ kg}$, and $m = 0.10 \text{ kg}$. Let the distance between $m_1$ and $m_2$ be $d = 2.0 \text{ m}$.

Let the particle $m$ be placed at a distance $x$ from $m_1$ towards $m_2$. For the net gravitational force on $m$ to be zero, the forces exerted by $m_1$ and $m_2$ must be equal in magnitude:

$\dfrac{G m_1 m}{x^2} = \dfrac{G m_2 m}{(d-x)^2}$

$\dfrac{2.00}{x^2} = \dfrac{4.00}{(2.0-x)^2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2.0-x}$

$2.0 - x = \sqrt{2} x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{2.0}{\sqrt{2}+1} = 2.0(\sqrt{2}-1) \approx 0.83 \text{ m}$

Thus, the particle should be placed $0.83 \text{ m}$ from the $2.00 \text{ kg}$ body towards the $4.00 \text{ kg}$ body.

The total gravitational potential energy $U$ of the three-particle system is the sum of the potential energies of all pairs:

$U = -G \left( $\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{d} + \dfrac{m_1 m}{x} + \dfrac{m_2 m}{d-x} \right)

Substituting the values ($x = 0.828 \text{ m}$ and $d-x = 1.172 \text{ m}$):

$U = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \left( \dfrac{2.00 \times 4.00}{2.0} + \dfrac{2.00 \times 0.10}{0.828} + \dfrac{4.00 \times 0.10}{1.172} \right)$

$U = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \left( 4 + 0.241 + 0.341 \right)$

$U = -6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4.582 \approx -3.06 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three particles, each having mass $m$, are positioned at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$. Determine the work that must be done on the system to increase the sides of the triangle to $2a$.
questions.solution:
The initial potential energy of the system is the sum of the gravitational potential energies of all three pairs of particles.

$U_i = -\dfrac{Gm^2}{a} - \dfrac{Gm^2}{a} - \dfrac{Gm^2}{a} = -\dfrac{3Gm^2}{a}$

The final potential energy of the system when the side length is increased to $2a$ is:

$U_f = -\dfrac{Gm^2}{2a} - \dfrac{Gm^2}{2a} - \dfrac{Gm^2}{2a} = -\dfrac{3Gm^2}{2a}$

The work done on the system by an external agent is equal to the change in the potential energy of the system.

$W = \Delta U = U_f - U_i$

$W = -\dfrac{3Gm^2}{2a} - $\$left(-\dfrac{3Gm^2}{a}\right)

$W = $\dfrac{3Gm^2}{a} - \dfrac{3Gm^2}{2a} = \dfrac{3Gm^2}{2a}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $100 \text{ g}$ is placed on the surface of a uniform sphere having a mass of $10 \text{ kg}$ and a radius of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine the work that must be done against their mutual gravitational force to move the particle far away from the sphere.
questions.solution:
The work done against the mutual gravitational force to move the particle to infinity is equal to the change in gravitational potential energy of the system.

$W = U_{\infty} - U_{\text{surface}}$

$W = 0 - \left( -\dfrac{GMm}{R} \right) = \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

Given:
$M = 10 \text{ kg}$
$m = 100 \text{ g} = 0.1 \text{ kg}$
$R = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^{2}/\text{kg}^{2}$

Substituting the values:

$W = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 10 \times 0.1}{0.1}$

$W = 6.67 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the gravitational field is given by $\vec{E} = (5 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{i} + (12 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{j}$. Determine the magnitude of the gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ placed at the origin.
questions.solution:
The gravitational field vector is given by $\vec{E} = 5 \hat{i} + 12 \hat{j}$ N/kg.

The magnitude of the gravitational field is:

$|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ N/kg

The gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $m$ is given by $\vec{F} = m\vec{E}$.

The magnitude of the gravitational force is:

$|\vec{F}| = m|\vec{E}|$

Substituting $m = 2$ kg and $|\vec{E}| = 13$ N/kg:

$|\vec{F}| = 2 \times 13 = 26$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the gravitational field is given by $\vec{E} = (5 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{i} + (12 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{j}$. Determine the potential at the points $(12 \text{ m}, 0)$ and $(0, 5 \text{ m})$ assuming the potential at the origin is zero.
questions.solution:
The relation between gravitational field $\vec{E}$ and gravitational potential $V$ is given by:

$dV = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$

Integrating from the origin $(0,0)$ to a point $(x,y)$:

$\int_{V(0,0)}^{V(x,y)} dV = -\int_{(0,0)}^{(x,y)} (E_x dx + E_y dy)$

Given $\vec{E} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$ and $V(0,0) = 0$, we get:

$V(x,y) - 0 = -\int_{(0,0)}^{(x,y)} (5 dx + 12 dy)$

$V(x,y) = -(5x + 12y)$

For the point $(12, 0)$:

$V(12, 0) = -(5 \times 12 + 12 \times 0) = -60 \text{ J/kg}$

For the point $(0, 5)$:

$V(0, 5) = -(5 \times 0 + 12 \times 5) = -60 \text{ J/kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the gravitational field is given by $\vec{E} = (5 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{i} + (12 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{j}$. Determine the change in gravitational potential energy when a particle of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ is taken from the origin to the point $(12 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$.
questions.solution:
The gravitational force on the particle is given by $\vec{F} = m\vec{E}$.

Substituting the given values:

$\vec{F} = 2(5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}) = 10\hat{i} + 24\hat{j} \text{ N}$

The displacement of the particle from the origin to $(12 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$ is:

$\Delta\vec{r} = 12\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} \text{ m}$

The work done by the gravitational field is:

$W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta\vec{r} = (10\hat{i} + 24\hat{j}) \cdot (12\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})$

$W = 10 \times 12 + 24 \times 5 = 120 + 120 = 240 \text{ J}$

The change in gravitational potential energy is the negative of the work done by the conservative gravitational force:

$\Delta U = -W = -240 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the gravitational field is given by $\vec{E} = (5 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{i} + (12 \text{ N/kg}) \vec{j}$. Determine the change in potential energy if a particle of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ is moved from $(12 \text{ m}, 0)$ to $(0, 5 \text{ m})$.
questions.solution:
The gravitational field is given by $\vec{E} = 5 \hat{i} + 12 \hat{j} \text{ N/kg}$.

The gravitational force on the particle of mass $m = 2 \text{ kg}$ is:
$\vec{F} = m\vec{E} = 2(5 \hat{i} + 12 \hat{j}) = 10 \hat{i} + 24 \hat{j} \text{ N}$

The initial position vector is $\vec{r}_i = 12 \hat{i} + 0 \hat{j} \text{ m}$ and the final position vector is $\vec{r}_f = 0 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j} \text{ m}$.

The displacement vector of the particle is:
$\Delta \vec{r} = \vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i = (0 - 12)\hat{i} + (5 - 0)\hat{j} = -12 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j} \text{ m}$

The work done by the gravitational force is:
$W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta \vec{r} = (10 \hat{i} + 24 \hat{j}) \cdot (-12 \hat{i} + 5 \hat{j})$
$W = 10(-12) + 24(5) = -120 + 120 = 0 \text{ J}$

The change in potential energy is equal to the negative of the work done by the conservative force:
$\Delta U = -W = 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The gravitational potential in a certain region is given by $V = 20 \text{ N/kg} \, (x + y)$, where $x$ and $y$ represent spatial coordinates in meters. What is the dimensional formula of the gravitational potential $V$?
questions.solution:
Gravitational potential $V$ is defined as the work done per unit mass.

$V = \dfrac{W}{m}$

The dimensional formula for work $W$ is $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$ and for mass $m$ is $[M]$.

Substituting these dimensions, we get:

$[V] = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[M]} = [L^2 T^{-2}]$

Alternatively, from the given equation, the unit of $V$ is $(\text{N/kg}) \times \text{m} = \text{J/kg}$.

The dimensional formula for Joule is $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$ and for kg is $[M]$.

Thus, $[V] = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[M]} = [L^2 T^{-2}]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The gravitational potential in a certain region is defined by $V = 20 \text{ N/kg} \, (x + y)$. Determine the gravitational field at a point $(x, y)$ in terms of the unit vectors $\vec{i}$, $\vec{j}$, and $\vec{k}$.
questions.solution:
The gravitational field $\vec{E}$ is related to the gravitational potential $V$ by the relation $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla} V$.

$\vec{E} = -\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} \vec{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} \vec{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} \vec{k} \right)$

Given $V = 20(x + y) = 20x + 20y$.

Differentiating partially with respect to $x$, $y$, and $z$:

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 20$

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = 20$

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = 0$

Substituting these values, we get:

$\vec{E} = -(20 \vec{i} + 20 \vec{j}) \text{ N/kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The gravitational potential in a specific region is given by $V = 20 \text{ N/kg} \, (x + y)$. Compute the magnitude of the gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $500 \text{ g}$ that is located at the origin.
questions.solution:
The gravitational field $\vec{E}$ is given by the negative gradient of the gravitational potential $V$:

$\vec{E} = -\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} \hat{k} \right)$

Given $V = 20(x + y)$, the components of the gravitational field are:

$E_x = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = -20 \text{ N/kg}$

$E_y = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = -20 \text{ N/kg}$

$E_z = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = 0$

The gravitational field vector is $\vec{E} = -20\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} \text{ N/kg}$.

The magnitude of the gravitational field is:

$|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{(-20)^2 + (-20)^2} = 20\sqrt{2} \text{ N/kg}$

The mass of the particle is $m = 500 \text{ g} = 0.5 \text{ kg}$.

The magnitude of the gravitational force acting on the particle is:

$F = m|\vec{E}| = 0.5 \times 20\sqrt{2} = 10\sqrt{2} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the gravitational field is specified by $\vec{E} = (2 \vec{i} + 3 \vec{j}) \text{ N/kg}$. Determine the work done by the gravitational field when a particle is moved on the line $3y + 2x = 5$.
questions.solution:
Given gravitational field $\vec{E} = 2 \hat{i} + 3 \hat{j}$ N/kg.

The gravitational force on a particle of mass $m$ is $\vec{F} = m\vec{E} = m(2 \hat{i} + 3 \hat{j})$.

The particle is moved along the line $2x + 3y = 5$.

Differentiating the equation of the line, we get $2 dx + 3 dy = 0$.

The work done by the gravitational field for a small displacement $d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j}$ is $dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = m(2 dx + 3 dy)$.

Since $2 dx + 3 dy = 0$, we have $dW = 0$.

Therefore, the total work done by the gravitational field is $0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the height above the earth's surface at which the weight of a body decreases to half of its value at the surface. (Let $R$ be the radius of the earth)
questions.solution:
The weight of a body at the surface of the earth is $W = mg$.

The weight of the body at a height $h$ above the earth's surface is $W_h = mg_h$.

Given that $W_h = \dfrac{W}{2}$, we have $g_h = \dfrac{g}{2}$.

The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ is given by $g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$.

Substituting $g_h = \dfrac{g}{2}$, we get:

$\dfrac{g}{2} = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2 = 2$

$1 + \dfrac{h}{R} = \sqrt{2}$

$\dfrac{h}{R} = \sqrt{2} - 1$

$h = (\sqrt{2} - 1) R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the acceleration due to gravity at the summit of Mount Everest, which is the highest mountain peak in the world with an elevation of $8848 \text{ m}$. The value of gravity at sea level is $9.80 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the Earth is given by the formula:

$g' = g \left(1 - $\dfrac{2h}{R}\right)

where $R$ is the radius of the Earth ($R \approx 6.37 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$) and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at sea level.

Given:
$h = 8848 \text{ m}$
$g = 9.80 \text{ m/s}^2$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$g' = 9.80 \left(1 - \dfrac{2 \times 8848}{6.37 \times 10^6}\right)$

$g' = 9.80 \left(1 - $\dfrac{17696}{6370000}\right)

$g' = 9.80 (1 - 0.00277)$

$g' = 9.80 \times 0.99723$

$g' \approx 9.77 \text{ m/s}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the acceleration due to gravity inside a mine at a depth of $640 \text{ m}$, assuming the surface value is $9.800 \text{ m/s}^2$. The radius of the earth is $6400 \text{ km}$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ is given by the formula:

$g_d = g \left(1 - $\dfrac{d}{R}\right)

Substituting $g = 9.800 \text{ m/s}^2$, $d = 640 \text{ m} = 0.64 \text{ km}$, and $R = 6400 \text{ km}$:

$g_d = 9.800 \left(1 - \dfrac{0.64}{6400}\right)$

$g_d = 9.800 \left(1 - $\dfrac{1}{10000}\right)

$g_d = 9.800 (1 - 0.0001)$

$g_d = 9.800 \times 0.9999$

$g_d = 9.79902 \text{ m/s}^2$

Rounding to three decimal places, the value is $9.799 \text{ m/s}^2.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Using a spring balance, a body is found to weigh $1.000 \text{ kg}$ at the north pole. Determine its weight at the equator, considering only the effect of the earth's rotation.
questions.solution:
The weight of the body at the north pole is given by $W_p = mg = 1.000 \text{ kg}$.

At the equator, the effective acceleration due to gravity is reduced by the centrifugal acceleration due to the Earth's rotation. The effective gravity is $g' = g - R\omega^2$.

The weight at the equator is $W_e = m(g - R\omega^2) = mg \left(1 - $\dfrac{R\omega^2}{g}\right) =$W_p\left(1 - $\dfrac{R\omega^2}{g}\right).

Substituting the known standard values:
Radius of Earth, $R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Angular velocity of Earth, $\omega = $\dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{24 \times 3600} \approx$7.27 \times 10^{-5} \text{ rad/s}$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

Calculating the centrifugal term:
$R\omega^2 = (6.4 \times 10^6) \times (7.27 \times 10^{-5})^2 \approx 0.0338 \text{ m/s}^2$

The fractional change in weight is:
\dfrac{R\omega^2}{g} = \dfrac{0.0338}{9.8} \approx$0.00345$

Therefore, the weight at the equator is:
$W_e = 1.000 \times (1 - 0.00345) = 1.000 - 0.00345 = 0.99655 \text{ kg}$

Rounding to three decimal places, we get $0.997 \text{ kg}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assuming the earth to be spherical, a body stretches a spring by a certain length on the earth's surface at the equator. At what height above the south pole will it stretch the same spring by the exact same length?
questions.solution:
The effective acceleration due to gravity at the equator is given by:

$g_{e} = g - \omega^2 R$

where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the poles, $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the earth, and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the south pole (where centrifugal force is zero) is:

$g_{h} = g \left(1 - $\dfrac{2h}{R}\right) (assuming $h \ll R$)

Since the spring is stretched by the same length, the effective gravity at both locations must be equal:

$g_{e} = g_{h}$

$g - \omega^2 R = g - $\dfrac{2gh}{R}

$\omega^2 R = $\dfrac{2gh}{R}

$h = $\dfrac{\omega^2 R^2}{2g}

We know that $\omega = $\dfrac{2\pi}{T}, where $T = 24 \times 3600 \text{ s}$. Substituting the standard values $R \approx 6400 \text{ km} = 6.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ and $g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$h = $\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{24 \times 3600}\right)^2 \times (6.4 \times 10^6)^2}{2 \times 9.8}

$h \approx $\dfrac{5.29 \times 10^{-9} \times 40.96 \times 10^{12}}{19.6}

$h \approx 11055 \text{ m} \approx 11 \text{ km}$

The closest value among the given options is $10 \text{ km}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the rate at which the earth must rotate so that the apparent $g$ at the equator becomes zero. What will be the length of the day in this situation?
questions.solution:
The apparent acceleration due to gravity at the equator is given by

$g' = g - R\omega^2$

For the apparent gravity to be zero, $g' = 0$

$g - R\omega^2 = 0$

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}$

Substituting $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{6.4 \times 10^6}} = 1.237 \times 10^{-3} \text{ rad/s}$

The length of the day in this situation will be

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$

$T = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{1.237 \times 10^{-3}} = 5077 \text{ s}$

Converting into hours

$T = \dfrac{5077}{3600} \text{ h} = 1.41 \text{ h}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum having a bob of mass $m$ hangs in a ship that is sailing along the equator from east to west. The angular speed of the earth's rotation is $\omega$ and the radius of the earth is $R$. Determine the speed of the ship due to the rotation of the earth about its axis, assuming the ship is stationary with respect to the water.
questions.solution:
The earth rotates about its axis with an angular speed $\omega$.

When the ship is stationary with respect to the water, it is at rest relative to the surface of the earth. Therefore, it moves along with the earth in a circular path of radius $R$ (the radius of the earth at the equator).

The speed of the ship in an inertial frame due to the rotation of the earth is simply the tangential speed of a point on the equator.

This speed is given by $v = \omega R$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum having a bob of mass $m$ hangs in a ship that is sailing along the equator from east to west. When the ship is stationary with respect to the water, the tension in the string is $T_0$. The angular speed of the earth's rotation is $\omega$ and the radius of the earth is $R$. Determine the magnitude of the difference between $T_0$ and the earth's attraction on the bob.
questions.solution:
When the ship is stationary with respect to the water, it is at rest relative to the Earth. The bob moves in a circular path of radius $R$ along with the Earth, rotating with angular speed $\omega$.

The forces acting on the bob are the true gravitational attraction of the Earth $F_g$ directed towards the center of the Earth, and the tension in the string $T_0$ directed away from the center.

The net force provides the necessary centripetal acceleration for the circular motion of the bob:

$F_g - T_0 = m \omega^2 R$

The magnitude of the difference between the tension $T_0$ and the Earth's attraction $F_g$ is:

$|F_g - T_0| = m \omega^2 R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum having a bob of mass $m$ hangs in a ship that is sailing along the equator from east to west. When the ship is stationary with respect to the water, the tension in the string is $T_0$. The angular speed of the earth's rotation is $\omega$ and the radius of the earth is $R$. If the ship sails at a speed $v$, what is the approximate tension in the string?
questions.solution:
Let the true acceleration due to gravity be $g$. The earth rotates from west to east with an angular speed $\omega$.

When the ship is stationary with respect to the water, it moves along with the earth from west to east with a speed $v_e = \omega R$. The equation of motion for the pendulum bob in the inertial frame (center of the earth) is:

$mg - T_0 = \dfrac{m v_e^2}{R} = m \omega^2 R$

$\Rightarrow T_0 = mg - m \omega^2 R$

When the ship sails from east to west at a speed $v$, its net absolute speed in the inertial frame becomes $v' = \omega R - v$. The new equation of motion is:

$mg - T = \dfrac{m (\omega R - v)^2}{R}$

$mg - T = m \omega^2 R - 2m \omega v + \dfrac{m v^2}{R}$

$\Rightarrow T = mg - m \omega^2 R + 2m \omega v - \dfrac{m v^2}{R}$

Substituting $T_0 = mg - m \omega^2 R$, we get:

$T = T_0 + 2m \omega v - \dfrac{m v^2}{R}$

Since the speed of the ship $v$ is much smaller than the equatorial speed of the earth $\omega R$, the term $\dfrac{m v^2}{R}$ is negligibly small and can be ignored.

$\Rightarrow T \approx T_0 + 2m \omega v$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Mars takes $1.88$ years to revolve around the sun. Determine the ratio of the average distance between Mars and the sun to that between the earth and the sun.
questions.solution:
Using Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period of revolution is directly proportional to the cube of the average distance from the sun:

$T^2 \propto R^3$

$\Rightarrow \left(\dfrac{T_M}{T_E}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{R_M}{R_E}\right)^3$

Given $T_M = 1.88$ years and $T_E = 1$ year.

\left(\dfrac{1.88}{1}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{R_M}{R_E}\right)^3$

$\dfrac{R_M}{R_E} = (1.88)^{2/3}$

$\dfrac{R_M}{R_E} = (3.5344)^{1/3} \approx 1.52

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a nearly circular orbit of radius $3.84 \times 10^5 \text{ km}$, the moon takes approximately $27.3$ days to revolve around the earth. Determine the mass of the earth using these data.
questions.solution:
The time period of a satellite revolving in a circular orbit of radius $R$ around a central body of mass $M$ is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{GM}}$

Squaring both sides and rearranging for $M$, we get:

$M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 R^3}{GT^2}$

Given values are:
$R = 3.84 \times 10^5 \text{ km} = 3.84 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$
$T = 27.3 \text{ days} = 27.3 \times 24 \times 3600 \text{ s} = 2.36 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$
$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$M = \dfrac{4 \times (3.14)^2 \times (3.84 \times 10^8)^3}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (2.36 \times 10^6)^2}$

$M = \dfrac{39.44 \times 56.62 \times 10^{24}}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.57 \times 10^{12}}$

$M = \dfrac{2233 \times 10^{24}}{371.5}$

$M \approx 6.02 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite of Mars travelling in an orbit of radius $9.4 \times 10^3 \text{ km}$ requires $27540 \text{ s}$ to complete one revolution. Calculate the mass of Mars.
questions.solution:
The time period of a satellite revolving around a planet is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$

Squaring both sides, we get:

$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GM}$

Rearranging for the mass of Mars $M$:

$M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{G T^2}$

Given:
$r = 9.4 \times 10^3 \text{ km} = 9.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
$T = 27540 \text{ s}$
$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$

Substituting the values:

$M = \dfrac{4 \times (3.14)^2 \times (9.4 \times 10^6)^3}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (27540)^2}$

$M = \dfrac{4 \times 9.86 \times 830.58 \times 10^{18}}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 7.585 \times 10^8}$

$M = \dfrac{32758 \times 10^{18}}{50.59 \times 10^{-3}}$

$M \approx 6.48 \times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$

Rounding off to one decimal place, we get:

$M \approx 6.5 \times 10^{23} \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1000 ext{ kg}$ satellite is intended to orbit the earth at an altitude of $2000 ext{ km}$ above the earth's surface. Determine its speed in the orbit. The mass of the earth is $6 imes 10^{24} ext{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
The radius of the Earth is taken as $R = 6400 \text{ km}$.

The altitude of the satellite is $h = 2000 \text{ km}$.

The orbital radius of the satellite is $r = R + h = 6400 + 2000 = 8400 \text{ km} = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$.

The orbital speed of a satellite is given by the formula:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

Substituting the standard value of the gravitational constant $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ and the given mass of the Earth $M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}{8.4 \times 10^6}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{40.02 \times 10^{13}}{8.4 \times 10^6}}$

$v = \sqrt{47.64 \times 10^6} \text{ m/s}$

$v \approx 6.90 \times 10^3 \text{ m/s} = 6.90 \text{ km/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1000 ext{ kg}$ satellite is intended to orbit the earth at an altitude of $2000 ext{ km}$ above the earth's surface. Determine its kinetic energy. The mass of the earth is $6 imes 10^{24} ext{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
Mass of the earth, $M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$
Radius of the earth, $R = 6400 \text{ km} = 6.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Altitude of the satellite, $h = 2000 \text{ km} = 2 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Orbital radius, $r = R + h = 6.4 \times 10^6 + 2 \times 10^6 = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
Mass of the satellite, $m = 1000 \text{ kg}$
Gravitational constant, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$

The kinetic energy of a satellite in a circular orbit is given by:
$K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$

Substituting the values:
$K = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 1000}{2 \times 8.4 \times 10^6}$

$K = \dfrac{40.02 \times 10^{16}}{16.8 \times 10^6}$

$K \approx 2.38 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1000 ext{ kg}$ satellite is intended to orbit the earth at an altitude of $2000 ext{ km}$ above the earth's surface. Determine the potential energy of the earth-satellite system. The mass of the earth is $6 imes 10^{24} ext{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
The potential energy of the earth-satellite system is given by:

$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$

where $r$ is the distance of the satellite from the center of the earth.

Given:
$m = 1000 \text{ kg}$
$M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$
$R = 6400 \text{ km} = 6.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$
$h = 2000 \text{ km} = 2 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

Distance from the center of the earth, $r = R + h = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

Substituting the values:

$U = -\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 1000}{8.4 \times 10^6}$

$U = -\dfrac{40.02 \times 10^{16}}{8.4 \times 10^6}$

$U \approx -4.76 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1000 ext{ kg}$ satellite is intended to orbit the earth at an altitude of $2000 ext{ km}$ above the earth's surface. Determine its time period. The mass of the earth is $6 imes 10^{24} ext{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
Radius of earth, $R = 6400 \text{ km}$

Altitude of the satellite, $h = 2000 \text{ km}$

Orbital radius, $r = R + h = 6400 + 2000 = 8400 \text{ km} = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

Mass of earth, $M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$

The time period of the satellite is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$

Substituting the values ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$):

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{(8.4 \times 10^6)^3}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{592.7 \times 10^{18}}{40.02 \times 10^{13}}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{1.481 \times 10^6}$

$T = 2 \times 3.1416 \times 1217$

$T \approx 7646 \text{ s}$

Converting to hours:

$T = \dfrac{7646}{3600} \text{ hours} \approx 2.12 \text{ hours}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the radius of the circular orbit for a satellite travelling with an angular speed equal to the angular speed of the earth's rotation. The mass of the earth is $6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
The angular speed of the earth's rotation is $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, where $T = 24 \text{ hours} = 86400 \text{ s}$.

For a satellite in a circular orbit, the gravitational force provides the necessary centripetal force:

$\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r$

$r^3 = \dfrac{GM}{\omega^2} = \dfrac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}$

Substituting the given values $M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$, and $T = 86400 \text{ s}$:

$r^3 = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times (86400)^2}{4\pi^2}$

$r^3 \approx \dfrac{40.02 \times 10^{13} \times 7.465 \times 10^9}{39.48}$

$r^3 \approx 75.67 \times 10^{21} \text{ m}^3$

Taking the cube root:

$r \approx 4.23 \times 10^7 \text{ m} = 42300 \text{ km}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit with an angular speed equal to the angular speed of the earth's rotation. If the satellite is directly above the north pole at a certain instant, determine the time it takes to arrive over the equatorial plane. The mass of the earth is $6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.
questions.solution:
The angular speed of the satellite is equal to the angular speed of the Earth's rotation.

Let the angular speed of the satellite be $\omega$. The time period of the Earth's rotation is $T = 24 \text{ hours}$.

$\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{24} \text{ rad/hour}$

The satellite is in a circular orbit passing over the north pole. Since the center of any satellite's orbit must coincide with the center of the Earth, the orbit is a polar orbit.

The angular displacement from the north pole to the equatorial plane is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

The time $t$ taken by the satellite to reach the equatorial plane is given by:

$t = \dfrac{\theta}{\omega} = \dfrac{\pi/2}{2\pi/24}$

$t = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6 \text{ hours}$

The mass of the Earth is extraneous information and is not required for this calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the true weight of an object located in a geostationary satellite, assuming it weighed exactly $10.0 \text{ N}$ at the north pole.
questions.solution:
The true weight of an object at the north pole is given by the gravitational force:

$W = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2} = 10.0 \text{ N}$

For a geostationary satellite, the time period of revolution is $T = 24 \text{ hours} = 86400 \text{ s}$. The radius $r$ of its orbit is obtained from Kepler's third law:

$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GM}$

$r = \left( \dfrac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \dfrac{gR^2T^2}{4\pi^2} \right)^{1/3}$

Substituting $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, $R = 6.37 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$, and $T = 86400 \text{ s}$:

$r \approx \left( \dfrac{9.8 \times (6.37 \times 10^6)^2 \times (86400)^2}{4\pi^2} \right)^{1/3} \approx 4.22 \times 10^7 \text{ m}$

The true weight of the object in the geostationary satellite is the actual gravitational force acting on it at that distance from the center of the Earth:

$W' = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = W \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^2$

$W' = 10.0 \times \left( \dfrac{6.37 \times 10^6}{4.22 \times 10^7} \right)^2$

$W' \approx 10.0 \times (0.151)^2 \approx 10.0 \times 0.0228 \approx 0.23 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet has a radius $R_1$, and a satellite revolves around it in a circle of radius $R_2$. The time period of revolution is $T$. Determine the acceleration due to the planet's gravitation at its surface.
questions.solution:
Let $M$ be the mass of the planet.

The acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the planet is given by $g = \dfrac{GM}{R_1^2}$.

For a satellite revolving in a circular orbit of radius $R_2$, the time period $T$ is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R_2^3}{GM}}$.

Squaring both sides, we get $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 R_2^3}{GM}$, which yields $GM = \dfrac{4\pi^2 R_2^3}{T^2}$.

Substituting this value of $GM$ into the expression for $g$, we obtain $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 R_2^3}{T^2 R_1^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is fired vertically upward with a speed of $15 \text{ km/s}$. Determine the speed with which it will travel in interstellar space, assuming only the earth's gravitational field is present.
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy at the surface of the earth is equal to the total energy in interstellar space (at infinity).

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 + 0$

The escape velocity $v_e$ from the surface of the earth is given by $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} \approx 11.2 \text{ km/s}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2$.

Substituting this into the energy equation gives:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2$

$v_f = \sqrt{v_i^2 - v_e^2}$

Given $v_i = 15 \text{ km/s}$ and $v_e = 11.2 \text{ km/s}$, we get:

$v_f = \sqrt{15^2 - 11.2^2}$

$v_f = \sqrt{225 - 125.44} = \sqrt{99.56}$

$v_f \approx 10 \text{ km/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is launched vertically upward from the surface of the earth and reaches a maximum height of $6400 \text{ km}$. Determine the initial speed of the particle.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

Given that the maximum height $h = 6400 \text{ km}$, which is equal to the radius of the earth $R$.

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}} = \sqrt{gR}$

We know that the escape velocity from the surface of the earth is $v_e = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2 \text{ km/s}$.

Therefore, $v = \dfrac{v_e}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{11.2}{1.414} \approx 7.9 \text{ km/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the minimum colatitude that can directly receive a signal from a geostationary satellite.
questions.solution:
The radius of the Earth is $R = 6400\text{ km}$.

The height of a geostationary satellite above the Earth's surface is $h \approx 36000\text{ km}$.

The distance of the satellite from the center of the Earth is $r = R + h = 6400 + 36000 = 42400\text{ km}$.

Let the maximum latitude that can directly receive the signal be $\lambda$. At this latitude, the line of sight from the satellite is tangent to the Earth's surface, forming a right-angled triangle with the Earth's center.

From the geometry of this triangle, we have:
$\cos \lambda = \dfrac{R}{r}$

Colatitude $\theta$ is defined as the angle measured from the pole, which is related to latitude by $\theta = 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}} - \lambda$.

Therefore, we can write:
$\sin \theta = \sin(90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}} - \lambda) = \cos \lambda = \dfrac{R}{r}$

Substituting the values:
$\sin \theta = \dfrac{6400}{42400} = \dfrac{8}{53} \approx 0.15$

Thus, the minimum colatitude is:
$\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.15)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass of $6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$ (equivalent to the mass of the earth) is to be compressed into a sphere such that the escape velocity from its surface reaches $3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$. Determine the required radius of the sphere.
questions.solution:
The escape velocity from the surface of a sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by:

$v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$

Rearranging the formula to solve for the radius $R$:

$R = \dfrac{2GM}{v_e^2}$

Substituting the given values $M = 6 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $v_e = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$, and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2\text{/kg}^2$:

$R = \dfrac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}{(3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$R = \dfrac{80.04 \times 10^{13}}{9 \times 10^{16}}$

$R = 8.89 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

$R \approx 9 \text{ mm}$
